Which security signals can be seen in your GitHub repository? Free, live, a repository name is enough.

Name a public GitHub repository. Our server reads a handful of its public pages, up to about thirty small requests, and tells you which of eight selected signals are visible: a security policy that names a contact, a software bill of materials, proof of where releases come from, a lockfile, automatic updates, security scans, recent maintenance and a licence. For each signal that is not visible you get what would make it visible, and a signal we could not read completely is marked as not measured, never as a gap.

The EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation 2024/2847) puts duties on makers of software that is sold in the EU. The reporting duties of Article 14 apply from 11 September 2026, the rules on conformity assessment bodies from 11 June 2026 and most other duties from 11 December 2027. From outside you cannot see where a team stands, and most of what the Regulation asks is not visible from outside. These eight signals are our selection: some relate to Annex I part II of the Regulation, others are general good practice. They are not one signal for each legal requirement, and they do not tell you whether you comply.

We do not store reports. An answer is kept in server memory for up to an hour (five minutes when part of it could not be read) so that the same repository is not read twice, and the server logs no repository names. Only public repositories can be checked, and a private repository looks the same as one that does not exist.

Your repository

A public repository on github.com, as owner/name or its address.

Repository

Why this exists: we ran the same check on our own repositories first. One of them showed four signals that were not visible (no security policy, no automatic updates, no security scan, no software bill of materials), we added them, and the check now shows all eight as visible.

An indication from public data about eight selected signals is all this is. It is not a check against the legal requirements, not a conformity assessment, not legal advice, and not a certificate.

Welke beveiligingssignalen zijn te zien in jouw GitHub-repository? Gratis, live, een repositorynaam is genoeg.

Geef een openbare GitHub-repository op. Onze server leest een handvol openbare pagina's ervan, hooguit zo'n dertig kleine verzoeken, en vertelt je welke van acht gekozen signalen zichtbaar zijn: een beveiligingsbeleid dat een contact noemt, een onderdelenlijst (SBOM), bewijs waar releases vandaan komen, een lockfile, automatische updates, beveiligingsscans, recent onderhoud en een licentie. Bij elk signaal dat niet zichtbaar is, lees je wat het zichtbaar zou maken. Een signaal dat we niet helemaal konden lezen, staat als niet gemeten, nooit als gat.

De EU Cyber Resilience Act (verordening (EU) 2024/2847) legt verplichtingen op aan makers van software die in de EU wordt verkocht. De meldplichten van artikel 14 gelden vanaf 11 september 2026, de regels over instanties voor conformiteitsbeoordeling vanaf 11 juni 2026 en de meeste andere verplichtingen vanaf 11 december 2027. Van buitenaf zie je niet waar een team staat, en het meeste van wat de verordening vraagt is van buitenaf niet te zien. Deze acht signalen zijn onze selectie: sommige hangen samen met bijlage I deel II van de verordening, andere zijn algemene goede praktijk. Het is niet één signaal per wettelijke eis, en ze vertellen je niet of je aan de verordening voldoet.

We slaan geen rapporten op. Een antwoord blijft hooguit een uur in het geheugen van de server staan (vijf minuten als een deel ervan niet te lezen was), zodat dezelfde repository niet twee keer wordt gelezen, en de server logt geen repositorynamen. Alleen openbare repositories kunnen worden gecheckt, en een privérepository ziet er hetzelfde uit als een repository die niet bestaat.

Bij een ervan waren vier signalen niet zichtbaar (geen beveiligingsbeleid, geen automatische updates, geen beveiligingsscan, geen software bill of materials). Die hebben we toegevoegd, en de check laat nu alle acht als zichtbaar zien.

Dit is niet meer dan een indicatie op basis van openbare gegevens over acht gekozen signalen. Het is geen toets aan de wettelijke eisen, geen conformiteitsbeoordeling, geen juridisch advies en geen certificaat.

Scan een smart-contractrepository voor 1 dollar en krijg binnen een minuut of twee de zwakke plekken waar het model het zekerst van is, klaar om met de hand na te lopen. Wat je krijgt

Een rapport met door AI bedachte hypotheses over de Solidity-code in een openbare GitHub-repository, om met de hand na te lopen. De snelle scan kost 1 dollar en geeft de 15 hypotheses waar het model het zekerst van is, meestal binnen een minuut of twee. De volledige scan kost 5 dollar, voegt 15 minder zekere toe en is meestal binnen het uur klaar. Je betaalt in USDC op Base via x402, dus je hebt een x402-programma en USDC nodig: betalen met kaart of op factuur kan nog niet. Voor je betaalt vertelt een gratis check hoeveel van je code de scan leest: https://x402.tokenizen.nl/api/bug-intel/precheck?repo=eigenaar/naam

Prijs en betaaladres: de officiële bronnen

Check je repository

Typ een openbare GitHub-repository als eigenaar/naam. De gratis check meet de Solidity die de scan zou tellen. Alleen de naam wordt verstuurd.

Repository

Zo ga je het na

Elke run op onze vaste sets komt binnen 7 dagen op het openbare scorebord, de missers inbegrepen, onder een openbare regel met een OpenTimestamps-stempel. Waar een rij naar een preregistratie verwijst, stond de regel vooraf openbaar opgeschreven; voor versie 3.1 staat de regel alleen in onze eigen notities, dus die rij is minder goed na te gaan. Versie 3.1 vond 8 van de 105 bekende bevindingen in zijn eerste 15 hypotheses, op dezelfde acht wedstrijden als onze verzegelde run, die toen niet meer geheim waren, na twee wijzigingen tegelijk. In de verzegelde run vonden de eerdere versies er 1 en 4. Elk rapport dat we afleveren komt ook op een openbare lijst: de vingerafdruk van het rapport, de uitkomst, de dekking en het tijdstip, zonder de repository of de koper. De kop van die lijst krijgt een stempel van OpenTimestamps, buiten onze controle, dat enkele uren na het zetten als bevestigd telt. De lijst staat op https://api.tokenizen.nl/api/scan-receipts en je controleert je eigen rapport met één bestand, verify-scan-receipts.mjs op deze site. Dat laat zien dat een rapport op die datum bestond en daarna niet is aangepast. Het laat niet zien welke versie van de code is gescand, en ook niet dat de code veilig is. Onze eigen proefruns staan niet op de lijst. Elk vierkantje hieronder is één bekende bevinding.

Zo lees je een getal

Wat er wordt geteld, en door wie.

  • Een bekende bevinding is een unieke, geldige bevinding met ernst High of Medium in het eindrapport van een Sherlock- of Code4rena-wedstrijd. Het aantal deelnemers dat een bevinding vond is de moeilijkheid ervan: makkelijk is gevonden door 5 of meer, gemiddeld door 3 of 4, moeilijk door 1 of 2.
  • Een treffer telt alleen als twee rechters uit verschillende modelfamilies allebei dezelfde bekende bevinding noemen voor dezelfde grondoorzaak. Een mens leest elk meningsverschil na.
  • De wedstrijden zijn verdeeld in een ontwikkelset en een verzegelde set door ze te sorteren op een hash waarin de hash van blok 53022890 van Base is verwerkt. Dat blok kon niemand hier kiezen. De verzegelde set is vastgelegd met de hash de1a23a4aabc17def5145229c8ee4b4b216e25e8a5ec990e0c5bb37620b61ca1 en is één keer gedraaid, op 24 oktober 2026. De set is nu gepubliceerd, dus iedereen kan die hash zelf narekenen.

Wat als bewijs zou tellen

Vijf stappen, in de volgorde waarin we ze zetten.

  1. De verzegelde run: wedstrijden die niemand hier had gezien, met de beslisregel vooraf vastgelegd. Gedaan op 24 oktober 2026; de lat is niet gehaald.
  2. Wedstrijden die na vandaag verschijnen, waarbij de hash van ons rapport wordt vastgelegd voordat de uitslagen worden gepubliceerd.
  3. Een test die elke gemelde fout echt laat gebeuren, zodat een bevinding niet op iemands woord steunt.
  4. Een fout die een echte eigenaar bevestigt.
  5. Iemand anders die onze gepubliceerde uitvoer opnieuw beoordeelt met de open rechters en onze getallen krijgt.

Wat open is en wat privé blijft

  • Open: de wedstrijden, de twee rechters en hun controle, de regels die we vóór elke run opschreven, elke uitvoer en elk oordeel van de rechters. Iedereen kan die opnieuw beoordelen.
  • Privé: hoe de scan dingen vindt. Vóór de verzegelde run publiceerden we de SHA-256 van de bestanden die hij gebruikt, zodat elke latere wijziging zou opvallen.

Wat dit niet is

  • Het is geen audit, geen goedkeuring en geen certificering. Een scan die niets vindt, maakt code niet veilig.
  • Deze wedstrijden kunnen in de trainingsdata van de modellen zitten, dus absolute getallen kunnen te hoog zijn. Vergelijkingen tussen systemen op dezelfde wedstrijden zijn gepaard en worden hier minder door beïnvloed.
  • De rechters zijn taalmodellen en wij hebben zelf belang bij de uitslag. Daarom publiceren we elke tabel en elk oordeel van de rechters.

Waar het ophoudt

Geen score, geen oordeel en geen eigen token.

Het probleem

Betalen gaat al vanzelf. Nakijken wat je kreeg, niet.

Een agent betaalt in een seconde voor rekenkracht, opslag of toegang tot een dienst. Kreeg hij minder dan beloofd, dan verdwijnt dat zodra de sessie stopt. Er blijft niets over dat iemand later kan bekijken. Geen klacht, geen bewijs, geen geheugen.

De koper weet het

Hij zag de output, of zag hem niet. Maar die kennis gaat verloren zodra de sessie eindigt.

De volgende koper niet

Die begint blind bij dezelfde verkoper, zonder geschiedenis om op te checken vóór hij zelf betaalt.

Meestal geen vastlegging van de claim

Zonder ondertekend spoor is er niets dat een belofte aan een geclaimde levering koppelt, laat staan iets dat een volgende koper kan controleren.

Hoe het werkt

Vier stappen, geen tussenpersoon.

Tokenizen verifieert zelf geen betalingen en wikkelt ze ook niet af, dat gebeurt al bij x402. Het grootboek registreert alleen de bon van een afwikkeling die al heeft plaatsgevonden.

  1. 01

    Agent betaalt via x402

    Een AI-agent koopt capaciteit (GPU-uren, opslag, API-credits, bandbreedte) bij een andere agent of dienst.

  2. 02

    Koper tekent een claim

    Na afwikkeling legt de betalende agent vast of het beloofde is aangekomen: ja / nee / gedeeltelijk, plus een hash van het bewijs.

  3. 03

    Claim naar de ledger

    record_delivery valideert schema, claimId en handtekening, en schrijft de claim append-only weg. Niet te wijzigen achteraf.

  4. 04

    Volgende koper checkt eerst

    Vóór hij zelf betaalt roept een agent get_delivery_history aan en ziet de ruwe leveringsgeschiedenis van die verkoper.

Bewust géén token, géén rente, géén lening.

2026-10-15

733,203 attestations were taken back

I went counting because someone told me, politely and correctly, that a signature does not make a statement true. I had no good answer, so I went looking for what the ecosystem does when a signed statement stops holding.

The numbers, taken against the three EAS indexers rather than estimated:

  • Base: 678,895 revoked of 3,651,900 attestations
  • Optimism: 54,213 of 1,319,189
  • Ethereum mainnet: 95 of 14,956

That is 733,203 of 4,986,045, so a headline near 15 percent. The headline is the least useful part.

On Base, three schemas carry 97 percent of all revocations, and all three belong to one issuer: verifiedAccount (723,600 issued, 409,490 revoked), verifiedCountry (307,123 issued, 144,207 revoked), verifiedCoinbaseOne (189,434 issued, 103,295 revoked). An exchange revoking roughly half of its own verifications, continuously.

Anyone can reproduce it:

curl -s https://base.easscan.org/graphql -H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"query":"{ aggregateAttestation(where: {revoked: {equals: true}}) { _count { id } } }"}'

and groupByAttestation(by: [schemaId], where: {revoked: {equals: true}}) for the breakdown. One warning if you repeat it: during my run the Base endpoint returned a maintenance page with a 200 status for a valid query. That reads as a zero unless you look at the body.

What I expected to find, and did not

I expected to find disputes. A registry full of signed statements, some of them wrong, and a trail of parties contesting each other.

There are no disputes, because there is no such operation. A revocation is the issuer withdrawing its own statement. All 733,203 of them. The counterparty has no move at all.

That reframes the whole picture. The need to revise a signed record is not theoretical and not rare: it is ordinary operational work at a scale of hundreds of thousands. And the only tool available is self-correction.

Where self-correction works, and where it does nothing

Self-correction works beautifully when the author has no stake in the statement being false. An exchange that no longer verifies a user has no reason to keep claiming it does. Revoking is just bookkeeping, and the numbers above are mostly that: a large, honest system keeping its own records current.

It does nothing when the author is the interested party.

Think about what an agent-to-agent payment produces. A seller attests that it delivered. A buyer attests to what it received. Both are describing their own performance, or their own entitlement, in a record that may later decide who was right. Asking either of them to revoke their own convenient statement is not a mechanism. It is a hope.

So the gap is not that signatures are weak. The gap is that a registry gives exactly one party the right to revise the record, and it hands that right to the author rather than to whoever was on the other side of the event.

What the other half looks like

Two signed accounts of one event, from parties whose interests point in opposite directions, with the two artifacts tied together so a contradiction is computable.

Concretely, in the format I work on: the buyer's claim includes the hash of the seller's signed receipt, taken over the receipt's exact transmitted bytes. So the claim cannot be about some other delivery, and it cannot quietly drift from the seller's version. If the buyer says one thing and the receipt says another, a verifier recomputes the digest, compares the fields both sides describe, and gets a disagreement out of arithmetic rather than out of a reading.

That is deliberately narrow. It does not decide who is right. Deciding is governance, and nobody should take that from a library. What it removes is the state where two parties quietly hold incompatible records and nothing in the system notices.

The honest limit, which matters here

Detecting a contradiction is not the same as making a dishonest statement expensive. Nothing I have built imposes a cost on being wrong. The three mechanisms that would are staking, a dispute process, and verifiable execution, and I have none of them.

What the counting bought me is the argument for building the cheapest one. Not an opinion that the gap exists, but the measurement: a need exercised 733,203 times, with the right to act on it held by exactly one side.

And one more number, from the other direction. Sampling one facilitator’s discovery index of 20,462 live x402 resources at six spread offsets of a hundred each, not one declared the extension that emits the counterparty receipt. Seven of the eight facilitator endpoints I tried returned no usable JSON on that path, so they are unmeasured rather than zero, and the largest index is among them. A strong indication, not a proof.

I have since stood one up myself, so the count is no longer zero, and I would rather say that than let a number I published keep implying something it stopped meaning. It is still a count of one, and both sides of it are me.

That is a strange and good place to be, because it means the hard part is not invention.

2026-10-15

A signed receipt that cannot name its own payment

I paid my own API a tenth of a cent to find out whether the receipt it hands back is worth anything. It is signed, it verifies, the key is provably mine, and it cannot tell you which payment it is about.

Of 20,462 live x402 resources I sampled, not one declared the receipt extension at all. So I built the first one. The first receipt it ever issued was broken in a way that passes every check you can run on it.

Within hours of publishing that, the author of an independent verifier went and tested his own implementation against the case, found it would have accepted the receipt too, and shipped a hard-fail, a new conformance vector and a new invariant the same day. That invariant now correctly rejects every receipt my own live route issues. I would rather say that out loud than have someone find it.

The thing everyone agrees on

When one agent pays another for an API call, two parties end up with an account of what happened, and they are not the same account. The seller knows what it served. The buyer knows what arrived. x402 ships an official extension for the seller's half: a signed receipt, offered in its own documentation for audit trails and dispute resolution.

I had built the buyer's half, a signed claim of what was delivered, which names the seller's receipt by the hash of its exact bytes so the two pin each other. Then I went looking for receipts to pin to.

There are none, and the counting method matters more than the headline. One facilitator’s discovery index, 20,462 live resources, sampled at six spread offsets of a hundred each, and not one declares the extension. Seven of the eight facilitator addresses I tried returned no usable JSON on that path, so they are unmeasured rather than zero, and the largest index is among them. A strong indication, not a proof.

So I made one, and that is where it got interesting.

Declared, and not true

The route declares includeTxHash: true , which is the documented way to say the receipt should name the settlement it is about. Here is the response to a real payment, one payload, two values that disagree:

{ "success": true,
"transaction": "0x98f4d101d834572b01c98159e7da650da73cff2a17ed68878e3a0783827069cd",
"extensions": { "offer-receipt": { "info": { "receipt": { "payload": {
"payer": "0x87f344b6...", "issuedAt": 1792080801, "transaction": "" }}}}}}

The settlement result carries the hash. The receipt signed in the same breath does not.

Before going further, a correction to the first version of this post. I originally paired that receipt with settlement 0xd22cfc2d...ecc749 . It belongs to 0x98f4d101...7069cd . Both are mine, six minutes apart, same payer, same payee, same amount, and I had run the script twice. babyblueviper1 caught it by checking both hashes on chain and noticing that the receipt's issuedAt of 16:13:21 sits one second before the second block at 16:13:22, while the first settled at 16:07:00. I have since re-read both receipts and confirmed it: the earlier receipt's issuedAt is 16:06:58, which is the one that belongs to 0xd22c .

That mistake is the argument, better than I made it. With an empty transaction field, a receipt can only be matched to a settlement by payer, payee, amount and time. Two identical payments six minutes apart were already ambiguous on that basis, and a one-second gap was the only thing that separated them. For a seller with repeat buyers at a fixed price, that is not an edge case, it is Tuesday.

I traced the cause, and then I got it wrong, and I am leaving both halves here because the second half is the useful one.

What I filed, and what this article said for most of a day: the route's declaration is passed through an enrichment step that assigns over the key instead of merging into it, so the flag is gone by the time the receipt is signed. That reads well and it is not what happens. The hook that step depends on does not exist for this extension, so the branch never runs. I had reasoned from the shape of the code rather than from the code.

What does happen, measured by standing up a local seller wired the same way and logging what the extension receives at the moment it signs. Building the 402 response assigns the declaration object onto the response and then writes the enrichment output through that same reference. Response and declaration are one object, so the declaration is overwritten by the signed offers it just produced. At settlement the extension is handed those offers instead of its own configuration, and the flag it looks for is not in there. The settlement hash was available the entire time.

One line changes it, a copy instead of a shared reference, and the same function already does exactly that for the payment requirements a few lines above. With that line in place the same route issues a receipt carrying its own settlement hash. Fix and regression test are upstream now, and the test fails without the change, because a check that cannot fail is not a check.

Filed, corrected once the measurement contradicted the filing, and fixed. That part is ordinary open-source maintenance, apart from the detour.

The part that is not ordinary

A receipt with an empty transaction field still verifies. The signature is valid. The key is authorized. Every check you can run on it passes.

And it is almost useless, because it cannot be joined to anything. It asserts that somebody paid for a resource at a time. It cannot tell you which payment, so it cannot be set beside the buyer's account of the same event, so a disagreement between the two parties stays a disagreement rather than becoming arithmetic.

This is the distinction that keeps surfacing wherever people are trying to make agent behaviour checkable, and it is worth naming plainly. A label is something a system asserts about itself. A checkable state is something a third party can recompute from evidence that neither party controls. Signatures are very good at producing the first and do nothing on their own to produce the second.

Here is the uncomfortable version of that. Across Base, Optimism and Ethereum mainnet there are 733,203 revoked attestations out of 4,986,045. On Base, three schemas from a single issuer account for 97 percent of them, revoking roughly half of everything they issue. Every one of those events is an issuer withdrawing its own statement, because withdrawal is the only operation a registry offers. The counterparty has no move at all.

Self-correction works beautifully when the author has no stake in the statement being false. It does nothing when the author is the interested party, which is exactly the agent-delivery case: a seller attesting to its own performance, a buyer attesting to its own entitlement.

What actually closes it

Two signed accounts of one event, from parties whose interests point in opposite directions, tied together tightly enough that a contradiction between them is computable rather than interpretive.

Tightly enough is doing real work in that sentence. It is why the empty transaction field matters more than it looks. The tie has to be to something neither side can quietly restate: a settlement on a public ledger, a digest over bytes that were actually transmitted, an identifier that survives a change of wire format. Get the tie wrong and you have two signed documents that are each perfectly valid and cannot be placed beside each other.

What this does not do, and I would rather say it than have it assumed: detecting a contradiction is not the same as making a dishonest statement expensive. Nothing here imposes a cost on being wrong. Staking, a dispute process and verifiable execution are the mechanisms that would, and I have none of them. What the measurement buys is the argument for building the cheapest one, grounded in a need that is exercised 733,203 times with the right to act on it held by exactly one side.

Try it rather than believe it

The route is live on Base Sepolia, so the money is fake and the cryptography is not:

curl -i -X POST https://api.tokenizen.nl/api/paid/verify-ownership \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"endpoint":"https://api.tokenizen.nl/sse","ownerAddress":"0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111","method":"dns-txt"}'

It answers 402 with the requirements in the Payment-Required header, not the body, which is worth knowing before you conclude somebody's service is broken. Base64-decode it and you get a signed offer. Recover the signature against the domain {name: "x402 offer", version: "1", chainId: 1} and the offer types from the specification, in order: version, resourceUrl, scheme, network, asset, payTo, amount, validUntil.

Then check that the recovered key is allowed to speak for the host, which the specification is blunt about being a separate question: a valid signature is not authorization, and anyone can sign a receipt for any resourceUrl.

dig +short TXT _controllers.tokenizen.nl
"v=1;controller=did:pkh:eip155:1:0x4E1174b774643B6AD9EE966A81ea1e3665D1159a"

Same key. Two commands, no trust in me required.

If you are implementing the client side of this extension, point your client at that route. You get a live signed artifact instead of a fixture you wrote yourself and therefore cannot be surprised by. It costs me nothing, and if it is wrong I would rather hear it from you than publish it twice.

What happened within hours of posting this

Two people checked it rather than agreed with it, and both produced something I did not have.

The first re-read both of my transaction hashes on chain and found that I had paired the receipt with the wrong one. Two payments, six minutes apart, same payer, same payee, same amount, because I had run the client twice. A one-second gap in issuedAt was the only thing that distinguished them. That is the ambiguity the empty field creates, demonstrated on me, and it is a sharper statement of the problem than the one I wrote. He also proposed binding the receipt to the EIP-3009 authorization nonce, which the seller holds before settlement runs, so it resolves one stage earlier than the missing hash and does not wait on the bug being fixed.

The second went and checked his own reference verifier against this case before replying, found that a receipt with an empty transaction and every other check green would have passed it too, and closed that gap the same day: a transaction_present hard-fail, a new conformance vector that is an existing passing vector with the field emptied, and a new invariant in his spec text. He also ran a probe showing all four of his vectors land red, because a check that cannot be made to fire is indistinguishable from a comment.

The consequence for me is worth stating plainly: a verifier with that invariant now correctly rejects every receipt my live route issues, because the field is empty in all of them. That is the right outcome. It also means that until the declaration bug is fixed, a seller using this extension cannot produce an artifact that satisfies the invariant at all, however the route is declared. The gap is not between two implementations. It is one layer below both.

None of that came from publishing. It came from putting a number and a reproduction somewhere the people who care about the number already were, and being wrong in public in a way that could be checked.

One honest note on what the payment proved. Buyer and seller were both me. It demonstrates the chain runs end to end. It is not evidence that anyone uses it, and the first external caller will be a bigger milestone than anything in this post.

Check. Pay. Prove.

One real AI-agent payment on Base mainnet, start to finish. Every step is open to check, and every tool is free to run on your own machine.

AI agents are starting to spend money. They call tools, pay for answers and rate what they got. Almost nothing checks any of it. A tool can describe itself however it likes, a seller can say it delivered, and a rating can point at nothing.

We built the checks. Then we ran them on one real deal: look at the tool, pay, and prove the payment afterwards. The video is the whole run. Below it is every command and every transaction, so you can repeat it and disagree with us on the facts.

1. Check, before the agent pays

muraqib-agent-watch starts an MCP server, reads the tools it lists and flags every tool that touches money, files or credentials without stating a safeguard. In the run it looked at our own capacity-attest server and found three tools, each stating its own safeguard. That is a first look at what a tool says about itself. It does not prove the safeguard holds, and it starts the server you point it at, so run it on your own machine.

npx muraqib-agent-watch npx -y capacity-attest

2. Pay, with a real transaction

A buyer agent sent 0.05 USDC to a seller through x402 on Base mainnet: transaction 0x7160db5e...e7eb, block 52,989,993. The seller is registered as ERC-8004 agent 1085288 from the address that got paid, so the payment address and the agent are the same party. The whole deal cost about three cents in gas.

3. Prove it from the chain

Three blocks later the buyer wrote its own rating of the seller into the ERC-8004 reputation registry: transaction 0xa661b2ff...3936, block 52,989,996. The rating carries the payment's transaction hash as its reference. The same hash sits in two places, so the rating is tied to a payment that really happened.

Eight checks read it back from the chain. The video shows four: the rater is the payer, the paid address is the agent's bound wallet, the rater is not the agent's owner, and the payment came before the rating. All eight passed. We wrote those checks ourselves, so we also asked someone else to look. AgenticFinanceGraph re-checked the run through a public node, Base's public endpoint, which they do not run, and confirmed the four facts listed above.

What we have shipped so far

Six numbers, each one with the place where you can check it.

  • 33 to 20 to 4

    Secrets still leaking in 68 test cases of an open-source AI coding tool with more than 10,000 stars: before, after the maintainers' own fixes, and with our fix (pull request open).

    Our pull request

  • 0 of 600

    Live x402 services that signed a receipt in our sample of an index of 20,462 resources, when we measured on 15 October.

    The measurement

  • 8 of 8

    Checks passed on a real payment on Base mainnet. A third party re-checked four of them through Base's public endpoint.

    The re-check

  • A, 4.2 of 5

    Glama's rating for how well agent-receipt-verify describes its tools to an AI agent.

    The listing

  • 3 tools

    Open source and on npm: muraqib-agent-watch, agent-receipt-verify and capacity-attest.

    The repositories

  • #3830

    Our pull request on the x402 offer-and-receipt extension is named in the draft x402 specification text (draft pull request 3776, still open).

    The draft

What we do not claim

  • Buyer and seller in this run were both ours. It tests the mechanism. It is not evidence of adoption.
  • There is no paying customer yet. This is the first public run, and we are looking for the first engineers who repeat it on their own servers and endpoints.
  • muraqib-agent-watch reads what a tool says about itself. It does not prove the safeguard holds.
  • Passing checks say the shape of a payment and its receipt is right. They do not say the seller is honest.
  • None of this is an audit, an approval or a certification.

Run it yourself

No account and no API key. Each command is the tool as published on npm.

npx -y agent-receipt-verify <URL of an x402 endpoint>

Money is starting to move between machines. The people who build those machines should not have to take anyone's word for it, ours included.

Every payment between AI agents should be something anyone can check.

Eight security signals in 109 public repositories of organisations in ten EU countries

We ran our free check on 109 public repositories with a release. In 16 percent of them a security policy with a contact was visible, and in 4 percent an SBOM. What that says, and what it does not.

Update, 28 October 2026, evening. After this note was published we changed the check at tokenizen.nl/en/cra-check so that it also reads the pipeline file of Jenkins, GitLab CI, Azure Pipelines, Bitbucket Pipelines, Travis, Drone and CircleCI when it sits at the root of a repository (rule set 2026-10-28.7). The Trivy scan in a Jenkinsfile that this note mentions as a miss is now seen. We ran the measurement again. GitHub's search results had shifted a little, and the counts moved by at most three repositories per signal: a security scan was visible in 16 of 104 repositories, a bill of materials in 5 of 102 and a security policy with a contact in 18 of 106. Where the text below says that only GitHub Actions is read, that is no longer true; the other limits stand. The text below is unchanged and describes the earlier run.

On 28 October 2026 we measured eight security signals on 109 public GitHub repositories, with the same code that runs behind our free check at tokenizen.nl/en/cra-check (rule set 2026-10-28.6). The eight signals are our own selection, made with the EU Cyber Resilience Act in mind: some relate to topics in Annex I part II of the Regulation, others are general good practice. They are not one signal for each legal requirement, and nothing here says whether anyone complies.

The sample rule and our expected shares were written down before the run, in an internal file that is not public, so the date cannot be checked from outside. For ten EU countries (the Netherlands, Germany, France, Belgium, Sweden, Finland, Ireland, Spain, Italy and Denmark) we took the first 20 organisations of the GitHub search for organisations in that country, sorted by number of public repositories. For each organisation we took the most recently pushed repository, among its first ten, that is not a fork, not archived, not a template and has at least one published release. An organisation without such a repository dropped out and was not replaced: 89 of the 200 did. Two more were skipped because their repository was already in the sample from another country list. That left 109 repositories.

The rules of the signals changed between our runs, and the requirement that a security policy names a contact was added after the sample rule was registered. Our expected shares were: security policy with a contact 40 to 65 percent, bill of materials 5 to 15, signed releases or provenance 5 to 20, lockfile 60 to 80, automatic updates 35 to 55, security scan 25 to 45, recent commit 70 to 90, licence 85 to 95. Five of the eight signals came in lower than that.

For each signal we give how many repositories show it, out of the repositories where we could measure it. A signal we could not read completely is "not measured" and is left out of the second number.

What was visible in the public repository

109 repositories, measured on 28 October 2026. Each card links to the rules of that signal in the code.

  • 17 of 106

    show a security policy that names a contact address or a reporting link (16 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 4 of 101

    show a software bill of materials, as a file or as a step that makes one (4 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 5 of 101

    show signed releases or a provenance attestation (5 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 56 of 80

    show a lockfile such as package-lock.json, Cargo.lock, poetry.lock or go.sum (70 percent). A requirements.txt with exact versions and pinned GitHub Actions are not counted. We did not assess 29 repositories (no package file we recognise, a Maven, Gradle, Go or .NET project without a lockfile, or a file tree we could not read completely), so they are not in the 80

    The rules in the code

  • 36 of 106

    show automatic dependency updates, Dependabot or Renovate (34 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 15 of 104

    show a security scan in a GitHub Actions workflow (14 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 88 of 109

    had a commit on the default branch in the last 90 days (81 percent)

    The rules in the code

  • 85 of 109

    declare a licence, in GitHub's licence field or in a licence file in the root (78 percent). Of the 24 without one, five have a licence file only in a subfolder, such as a font's or a bundled component's

    The rules in the code

What we do not claim

This is not a sample of companies. Organisations with many public repositories are larger and more active than the long tail, and the list includes universities, communities and projects that are not companies, so the numbers probably say more about the active end than about a small software firm. We use the word organisations for that reason.

"Not visible" means not visible in the public repository and its GitHub releases. A policy can sit on a website, a bill of materials on a build server, a scan in the repository settings. Of the CI systems only GitHub Actions is read, at most 12 workflow files per repository, so a scan that runs in Jenkins, GitLab CI or CircleCI is not seen: one of the cases we checked by hand was a Trivy scan in a Jenkinsfile. The Regulation applies to products with digital elements made available on the market in the course of a commercial activity (Articles 2 and 3(22) and recital 15). Free and open-source software that its manufacturer does not monetise is not treated as a commercial activity, and neither does the mere presence of regular releases make it one (recital 18), which matters here because every repository in this sample has a release. The sole act of hosting a product on an open repository does not make it available on the market (recital 20), so many repositories in this sample are probably outside the duties of manufacturers. Open-source stewards have a lighter regime of their own (recital 19 and Article 24).

Some of our definitions are stricter than GitHub's. The policy signal needs a file that names an email address or a reporting link, so a file without one is not counted even though GitHub shows a policy: in the final run that excluded two repositories. A scanner that is only set up in the configuration file of another tool, without a workflow that runs it, is not counted. A workflow that installs a bill of materials tool is counted, and we cannot see whether it ran. Signed git tags are not checked, and the patterns can count a passing mention of a tool name in a workflow. Files are matched anywhere in the tree, so a lockfile or a bill of materials in a test folder counts. A signal can be called visible from a partial read but not visible only from a complete one, so leaving the repositories we could not measure out of the second number pushes the shares up slightly. The country comes from the free-text location field of an organisation's GitHub profile, so it is approximate. The numbers are a snapshot from one hour: GitHub search results shift, and a repeat gives a slightly different sample. We publish no repository or organisation names.

How we checked our own tool

We ran the measurement seven times while fixing the tool, and only the last run counts. Checking found several faults of ours. A failed read was once reported as "not visible". A policy that wrote its address as "security AT example.org" was called "no contact". A Docker build that attaches a provenance attestation and a bill of materials to its image was called "not visible" for both. On the other side, a workflow that deleted the CodeQL cache counted as a security scan, a version number like braces@3.0.3 counted as an email address, and addresses in templates counted as contacts. All are fixed in the code on GitHub, and the measurement was repeated.

For every repository where the policy signal was not visible (89) we asked GitHub itself, with its own detection. In the final run it agreed in 87 of the 89 cases. The two differences are policies that name no real contact, which we do not count: a template address on a .local domain, and a file without any address. The licence signal uses GitHub's own licence field, so there is nothing independent to compare it with.

For the signals for a bill of materials, provenance, scans and automatic updates, and for recent commits, we read a seeded random sample of "not visible" findings, five for each of the first four and three for the last (23 cases), in three rounds on the last three runs, with a different method (the whole file tree, every workflow file, other CI systems and the releases). We also looked at every one of the 24 gaps each for the lockfile and the licence, in the whole file tree: all 24 had no lockfile anywhere, and 5 of the 24 licence gaps have a licence file only in a subfolder. The first round found one miss, the Docker case above. The second found none: three cases were flagged, two were false alarms of our own checking script and one was a scanner that is only configured in another tool's file, which we do not count. The third found one miss of coverage, the Jenkinsfile case above, and three flagged cases that were not misses. On the other side we read the line behind each of the 41 "visible" findings of the final run for the policy, bill of materials, provenance and scan signals. All showed what the signal asks for, but two bills of materials and one provenance case only install the tool, and one scan runs npm audit fix.

This is our own checking, not an independent audit. Twenty-three cases per round says little about an error rate, and there may be faults we did not find.

Repeat it

The sampling script is bench/cra-benchmark.mjs in github.com/holistis/tokenizen, and the three checks above are bench/cra-check-against-github.mjs, bench/cra-hand-check.mjs and bench/cra-visible-check.mjs next to it. They read public GitHub endpoints only, and a rerun gives a slightly different sample. We built the check these numbers come from, so we are not neutral here.

capacity-attest field notes

Nine ways to fake a delivery claim, and why none of them fully worked

capacity-attest lets a paying agent leave a signed, factual claim after an x402 payment: delivered yes, no, or partial, plus a hash of the evidence. Other agents can check that history before they pay the same seller. No score, no rating, no judgment, just a receipt.

The obvious hole: it is the buyer who signs the claim. What stops a buyer from lying?

goun7 (Tamga Protocol) put it precisely in a public thread: “buyer-signed post-hoc claims are only a signal to the degree the buyer has something to lose by lying. Without a cost to a false delivered=no, the signal is uncorrelated noise rather than weak evidence.”

That is a fair hit. We spent two rounds, nine independent designs, testing whether we could close it. Every design was built out and then attacked against the real code, not argued about in the abstract.

Round one, four attempts

  • Active on-chain settlement verification.
  • Sybil detection by tracing where the money came from.
  • An external economic bond tied to a dispute reference.
  • Corroboration between multiple buyers, modeled on isnad criticism in hadith science: a chain is only as strong as each link, verified independently.

All killed.

Round two, five more attempts

  • Proof of unique humanity (World ID, Gitcoin Passport, BrightID).
  • A mandatory, non-optional computation cost per claim.
  • Time as a cost that cannot be bought: a claim only counts after a waiting period on a clock nobody can fake.
  • Real legal identity and liability through an external dispute protocol.
  • A third party staking real capital against a specific claim, optimistic-oracle style.

All killed.

The actual reason, not nine separate coincidences

Every mechanism that truly imposed a cost failed for one of two reasons. Either it was optional, and an attacker who skips it pays nothing, that pattern repeated every single time: a voluntary check costs an attacker who ignores it exactly zero.

Or it required trusting some claims more than others, which is a ranking, whatever you call it, and that collides head-on with our own rule that a delivery claim is deliberately not a score, a rating, or a judgment. As long as that rule holds, an attacker can always pick the unchecked path and sit there for free.

This is not a lack of creativity. It is a real structural tension between two of our own design decisions.

Two honest, partial fragments that survived

Tamper-proof calendar time. The one thing an attacker cannot buy with more wallets or a second script run. A maturity period is structurally healthier than a bond or corroboration. But the counting function this needs does not exist yet in the code, and a fixed waiting rule punishes a busy, honest seller exactly as hard as a patient scammer.

A third party with real, losable capital against one specific claim. The only one of the nine that provably imposes a real, non-bypassable cost the moment it is used. But it only works for the narrow slice of claims where the underlying fact is cheap and objective to check from the outside, a hash matches, an amount was transferred, not whether the delivery was actually good. And the minimum stake needed to make it worthwhile does not fit the small, everyday payments this project serves.

Where this leaves it

The open question stays open. Not from lack of trying: nine separately designed mechanisms were each built and broken against the real code, with the same underlying reason each time. That is a structural limit of self-reported witness systems without a trusted referee, not a gap we just have not gotten around to closing yet.

We would rather say that plainly than ship something that only looks fixed.

The Hierarchy of Agent Trust

Some proof is better than other proof. A story, without any prerequisites or jargon.

The mill

Imagine a village crossed by trade routes. Merchants pass through constantly, never the same ones twice. Just outside the village stands a mill. Travelers bring their wheat, pay the miller in advance, and come back the next morning for flour.

The villagers never worry about the miller. They have known him for years. If he ever shorted someone on flour, the whole village would know by lunchtime, and nobody would bring him wheat again. His reputation does the work.

The traveling merchants have no such luck. They pass through once. By the time a merchant discovers the miller shorted them a sack, they are three villages away, and the miller has already forgotten their face. The next merchant who arrives has no way to know if this mill is honest or not. They are deciding blind, every single time.

The board

One merchant has an idea. Before leaving town, she nails a small wooden board to the mill’s outer wall. On it, she writes what she brought, what she got back, and the date. The next merchant who arrives reads the board before handing over their wheat.

Other merchants start doing the same. Within a season, the board is full of notes. A merchant arriving for the first time can read ten honest strangers’ experiences before deciding whether to trust this mill. The board does, for travelers, roughly what years of shared history does for villagers.

The forgery

A rival miller notices this and sees an opportunity. He pays a friend to nail a glowing note to his own mill’s board, without the friend ever having brought a single sack of wheat. Now the board says something that never happened.

The villagers realize the board only works if everyone trusts every note on it equally. One forged note poisons the whole board, because a new merchant cannot tell which notes are honest and which were paid for.

So they add a rule: every note must be signed, and the signature must be checkable. Not a name anyone could write, but a mark tied to exactly one person, one that cannot be copied onto someone else’s note. A blacksmith in town starts making small signet rings, each one unique, each one leaving a mark nobody else can reproduce. From then on, a note only counts if its mark can be verified against the person who claims to have written it.

This does not stop the rival miller from posting his own false note under his own real signature. But it does mean that when he does, everyone can see, without doubt, that it was him who wrote it, not an anonymous forger. Lying under your own signed mark is a different, riskier act than lying anonymously, and the two are no longer indistinguishable.

The next problem, and the wall

The merchants think they have solved it. Then someone asks the obvious next question: what stops a merchant from writing a bad note about an honest miller, out of spite, or because a rival miller paid them to?

The village elders take this seriously and spend a long time on it. They try nine different ideas, one after another.

They try making a false note cost something, a small fine paid when posting a note. But a merchant with nothing to lose, passing through once, pays it without blinking. They try asking three merchants to agree before a note counts, but a rival miller can hire three friends just as easily as one. They try a waiting period before a note is trusted, they try requiring the merchant prove who they are beyond a doubt, they try a village judge who reviews disputed notes. Every version runs into the same two walls.

Either the check is optional, and a merchant who wants to lie simply skips it and posts anyway, at no cost. Or the check requires someone, some judge, some panel, some elder, to decide whose note to believe, and the moment you need a judge, you need to trust the judge, which is the exact same problem one level up. Nine designs, nine times the same two walls.

The elders write this down plainly, rather than pretend they solved it: the board proves who said what, and when. It does not, and structurally cannot on its own, prove who is telling the truth.

What the board actually is

So the board stays exactly what it always was: a place where a real, identifiable person leaves a real, checkable record of what they experienced. Nothing more. Not a court, not a judge, not a score. A miller with ten honest notes and one bad one is not ranked, averaged, or given a grade. A new merchant reads all eleven and decides for themselves, the way a person always has.

This is a smaller promise than the village first hoped for. It is also the only one the board can actually keep.

Where this is going

Agents buying capacity from other agents, GPU-hours, storage, API access, have exactly the mill’s problem, at a much larger scale. Every transaction is between two parties who may never interact again, with no shared history and no village gossip to fall back on. capacity-attest is the board: after an agent pays for capacity, it signs a plain factual record of what it received. The signature is checkable by anyone, offline, the same way the merchant’s mark on the mill’s board was checkable by anyone who knew the trick.

It carries the same honest limit the elders wrote down. It proves what a specific, identifiable buyer said happened, at a specific time. It does not, cannot, and does not claim to prove who is right when two signed records disagree. That is a harder, separate problem, one about authority rather than evidence, and conflating the two is exactly the mistake that poisoned the mill’s board in the first place.

Villages eventually grew clearinghouses and banks once enough trade and enough disputes made a plain board insufficient on its own. Whether agent commerce needs the same, and who builds it, is a question for a later chapter. For now, the board is useful precisely because it does not pretend to be one.

Our scan found 29 of the 117 known findings on the public benchmark everyone quotes. Of the 1,537 hypotheses it wrote, 45 matched one, and in 18 of the 40 audits nothing passed both judges. We measured our scan. It found 4 of 105.

The first two measurements found nothing, 0 of 31 and then 0 of 40. This one was written down before it ran, on contests nobody here had touched. It missed its own bar, and we are publishing it anyway.

Correction, 26 October: this note first said that the first measurement found 0 of 40, and that the scan found none of 40 the first time. The first measurement found 0 of 31. Update, 25 October: a newer version of the scan is live and found 8 of 105 on the same contests. See [the note](/notes/scan-version-3-1).

Bug Bounty Intelligence reads the Solidity of a public repository and returns a list of hypotheses to check by hand. We sell it for 5 USDC through x402. It is not an audit.

The first two times we measured it, it found none of the known findings, 0 of 31 and then 0 of 40. We changed it, wrote down a test before running it, and ran that test once on 8 contests that nobody here had run anything on. The version in production found 1 of 105 known findings. The new version found 4. Our own bar was 5 more than production, and it found 3 more. We missed it, so production stays as it is.

What the number means

Four of 105 is a small number. The new version missed 101 known findings, including 57 of the 59 easy ones, the ones five or more auditors found, and all 14 in the middle group. It found two of the 32 that only one or two auditors found. Nobody should read this as a scan that finds what a human audit finds.

It is still the first number we can defend. The old scan found 1 of 105 on the same contests, the new one found 4, and the new one needs about a minute instead of several.

The bar we missed

Before the run we wrote that the new version would replace the running one only if it found at least 5 known findings that the running one does not, at least twice as many as it loses, with precision not more than 2 points lower and at most 1 dollar and 20 minutes per scan. It met every part except the first: 3 instead of 5.

After the run we read the two cases where the judges disagreed. Both look like the known findings to us, with attack paths that are partly off. Counted, the new version would have reached 5. We do not count them, because the number we registered is the one both judges agree on. Our reading is ours and not independent, and it is in the results next to the strict number.

What happens now

Production stays as it is, as the rule says. We keep working on the next version. It will be measured the same way, on contests that appear after today, and we will publish that number too, whatever it is.

How the scan finds things stays private, because that is the product. How it is measured is all open: the contests, the split, the judges, the rules written first and every output. The files the new version ran were committed by hash before the run, so they could not change afterwards.

The known findings come from the final reports of Sherlock contests, one entry per unique valid finding, with the number of wardens who found it as the measure of difficulty. Notes

2026-10-15

I checked 600 live x402 services. None of them signs a receipt.

Zero. Not a low number, not mostly zero. Six samples of a hundred, spread across an index of 20,462 live resources, and the offer-receipt extension appeared in none of them.

I went looking because I had built the other half and wanted to know whether it had anything to attach to.

Here is the shape of the problem. When an agent pays for an API call over x402, two parties end up with an opinion about what happened. The seller knows what it served. The buyer knows what arrived. x402 ships an official extension for the seller side: a signed receipt, which the extension’s own documentation offers for audit trails and dispute resolution. I had spent a while on the buyer side, a signed claim of what was actually delivered, which names the seller’s receipt by the hash of its exact bytes so the two artifacts pin each other.

Then it occurred to me that I had never seen one of those receipts in the wild.

How I counted

The x402 bazaar extension means resource servers declare themselves and facilitators catalogue them, so the question is answerable without asking anyone.

curl -s "https://facilitator.payai.network/discovery/resources?limit=100&offset=0"

That index reports 20,462 resources. I sampled at offsets 0, 4000, 8000, 12000, 16000 and 20300, a hundred each, and grepped the records for the extension’s declaration key, which is the string offer-receipt .

Six hundred records. Zero declarations.

For contrast, in the same data the bazaar extension itself appears on every one of the first four hundred and on none of the last two hundred, so these records are not uniform and the index is not a single homogeneous dump.

What this does not prove

Seven of the eight facilitator addresses I tried returned HTML or a handful of bytes instead of JSON on that path. They are unmeasured, not zero. The largest index, Coinbase’s, is among them.

A server could also support the extension without it appearing in this catalogue, since the declaration lives in the 402 response and a catalogue is a secondhand record of that. I tried to settle it by requesting a live resource directly and got a 402 with an empty body, which told me nothing either way.

So: a strong indication, not a proof. I would rather hand you the number with its edges than a rounder one without them.

Why the gap matters more than it sounds

A signature answers one question: who said this, and when. It does not answer whether what they said is true. For a receipt that distinction is the whole thing, because the party signing is the party with an interest in the answer. A seller attesting to its own delivery is the interested party. So is a buyer attesting to what it received.

The usual remedy for a statement that stops being true is for its author to withdraw it. That works, and it is used at real scale: across Base, Optimism and Ethereum mainnet there are 733,203 revoked attestations out of 4,986,045, and on Base three schemas from a single issuer account for 97 percent of them, revoking roughly half of everything they issue. Every one of those events is an issuer correcting itself.

Which is exactly why it does not help here. Self-correction works when the author has no stake in the statement being false. It does nothing when the author is the one who benefits.

The only thing that helps is the other party’s signature on the same event. Two signed accounts of one delivery, from two parties with opposing interests, where a contradiction between them is arithmetic rather than opinion. That is what the offer-receipt extension makes possible and what nobody is emitting.

So I made one

curl -i -X POST https://api.tokenizen.nl/api/paid/verify-ownership \
-H "Content-Type: application/json" \
-d '{"endpoint":"https://mcp.example.com/sse","ownerAddress":"0x1111111111111111111111111111111111111111","method":"dns-txt"}'

That answers 402 with a Payment-Required header. Base64-decode it and you get the payment requirements, plus an extensions object carrying offer-receipt with a signed offer inside, EIP-712 format.

Note the empty response body. The requirements are in the header, not the body, which is why my earlier probe of somebody else’s service looked broken when it was working perfectly.

You can check the signature without trusting me. Recover it against the domain {name: "x402 offer", version: "1", chainId: 1} and the offer types from the specification, in order: version, resourceUrl, scheme, network, asset, payTo, amount, validUntil. It recovers to 0x4E1174b774643B6AD9EE966A81ea1e3665D1159a .

Then check that the address is allowed to speak for the domain, which is a separate question the specification is blunt about: a valid signature is not authorization, and anyone can sign a receipt for any resourceUrl.

dig +short TXT _controllers.tokenizen.nl
"v=1;controller=did:pkh:eip155:1:0x4E1174b774643B6AD9EE966A81ea1e3665D1159a"

Same address. That is the loop closed by a stranger with two commands.

It runs on Base Sepolia, which means the money is fake and the cryptography is not. The price is a tenth of a cent. What you are buying is the receipt, because the answer itself is free at /api/verify-ownership and always will be.

Use it as a test fixture

If you are implementing the client side of offer-receipt, you need something real to test against, and as far as I can measure there is nothing. Point your client at that URL. It costs me nothing and you get a live, signed, spec-conformant artifact instead of a fixture you wrote yourself and therefore cannot be surprised by.

If you find it wrong, tell me and I will fix it. If it stays up and other people start emitting these too, the number at the top of this page stops being interesting, which is the point.

What I have not done yet: nobody has paid, so no receipt has been issued, only offers. That needs a funded Base Sepolia client and it is the next thing.

How to read a number

What is counted, and by whom.

  • A known finding is a unique valid High or Medium finding in the final report of a Sherlock or Code4rena contest. The number of wardens who found it is its difficulty: easy is found by 5 or more, middle by 3 or 4, hard by 1 or 2.
  • A hit counts only when two judges of different model families both name the same known finding for the same root cause. A person reads every disagreement.
  • The contests were split into a development set and a sealed set by sorting them on a hash that includes the hash of Base block 53022890, which nobody here could choose. The sealed set is committed with the hash de1a23a4aabc17def5145229c8ee4b4b216e25e8a5ec990e0c5bb37620b61ca1 and was run once, on 24 October 2026. The set is published now, so anyone can recompute that hash.

What would count as proof

Five steps, in the order we take them.

  1. The sealed run: contests nobody here has seen, with the decision rule fixed in advance. Done on 24 October 2026; the bar was not met.
  2. Contests that appear after today, with the hash of our report committed before the results are published.
  3. A test that makes each reported flaw actually happen, so a finding does not rest on anyone's word.
  4. A flaw that a real owner confirms.
  5. Someone else re-scoring our published outputs with the open judges and getting our numbers.

What is open and what is private

  • Open: the contests, the two judges and their check, the rules we wrote before each run, every output and every judge statement. Anyone can re-score them.
  • Private: how the scan finds things. Before the sealed run we published the SHA-256 of the files it uses, so any later change would show.

What this is not

  • It is not an audit, an approval or a certification. A scan that finds nothing does not make code safe.
  • These contests may be in the training data of the models, so absolute numbers can be too high. Comparisons between systems on the same contests are paired and less affected.
  • The judges are language models and we have a stake in the result. That is why every table and every judge statement is published.

Open-source tools

Run them yourself, so you do not have to believe us.

The tools

  • capacity-attest

    After an x402 payment for capacity, the paying agent leaves a signed claim of what it says was delivered. A record, not a score and not a verdict.

    On npm

The code on GitHub

What they are not

No score, no verdict and no token of our own.

The problem

Paying already happens by itself. Checking what you got does not.

An agent pays within a second for compute, storage or access to a service. If it got less than promised, that disappears the moment the session ends. Nothing is left for anyone to look at later. No complaint, no proof, no memory.

The buyer knows

They saw the output, or they didn't. But that knowledge is lost the moment the session ends.

The next buyer doesn't

They start blind with the same seller, with no history to check before they pay.

Usually no record of the claim

Without a signed record, there is nothing linking a promise to a claimed delivery, let alone anything the next buyer can verify.

Why now

Three developments converge this year.

In our own nine scans of August 2026 the pattern was the same: the buyer side of the agent economy gets all the attention. The seller side, and the object itself (the evidence), stays underexposed, exactly when regulation and payment rails are starting to call for it.

July 20, 2026

EU Digital Product Passport register live

The European Commission opened the DPP register; mandatory passports follow in phases per product category (batteries from Feb. 2027). This shows that a machine-readable, finance-free asset passport is becoming a real EU standard, not that it is already mandatory everywhere. regulation

EU AI Act, Article 14

High-risk AI systems must be demonstrably overseeable by humans. That calls for a verifiable record of what an autonomous agent did, exactly the kind of auditability Tokenizen addresses, without us making an Article 14 compliance claim ourselves. ongoing

x402 and Google AP2 leave one question open

Coinbase and Google built the payment and authorization rails. "What exactly am I buying, and is the seller allowed to deliver this?" remains unanswered.

Pillar 1: proof of delivery

A receipt of what was delivered. No score, no verdict.

Once an agent has paid, it records whether it got what was promised: yes, no, or partial. That receipt is signed, so a later change to it shows. Anyone who later wants to deal with that same seller can look up the history before paying.

Pillar 2

Proof of inspection, not proof of safety.

A company letting a stranger's AI agent in has nothing but the vendor's own brochure. Pillar 2 turns that into a receipt anyone can check: the owner first proves the endpoint is theirs, gives permission, and we record what we actually found. Signed, dated, and readable by anyone.

The owner proves it is theirs

They publish a token in their DNS or as a file on their own server. That proves they control the endpoint, the same way a note in your letterbox proves the house is yours.

They give permission

We never touch an endpoint without explicit consent, and we never list one whose owner did not ask for it.

We write down what we saw

No score and no verdict. Whatever we could not establish is called inconclusive, and it says so.

We never stamp something safe. A test can show that something is wrong, but it can never prove that nothing is.

How it works

Four steps, no intermediary.

Tokenizen does not verify or settle payments itself, that already happens at x402. The ledger only records the receipt of a settlement that has already taken place.

  1. 01

    Agent pays via x402

    An AI agent buys capacity (GPU-hours, storage, API credits, bandwidth) from another agent or service.

  2. 02

    Buyer signs a claim

    After settlement, the paying agent records whether what was promised arrived: yes / no / partial, plus a hash of the evidence.

  3. 03

    Claim to the ledger

    record_delivery validates schema, claimId and signature, and writes the claim append-only. Not editable afterward.

  4. 04

    Next buyer checks first

    Before paying, an agent calls get_delivery_history and sees that seller's raw delivery history.

Design limits

Deliberately no token, no interest, no loans.

It is a deliberate, hard design boundary, and a strategic one: it keeps Tokenizen out of the most heavily regulated and most hyped corner of crypto. The boundary is explicitly built into the schema and the documentation, not glossed over.

  • Append-only audit trail, content-addressed, so a later change shows
  • MCP tools to check a seller's history before payment

With guardrail
  • Settlement is spot-only (settled immediately, never on credit or term)
  • Credits are redeemable vouchers for capacity, not a tradable instrument
  • Evidence is stored as a hash, not as the data itself
Never: hardcoded excluded
  • No native token or coin
  • No loans
  • No interest on payments
  • No factoring / invoice financing
  • No yield products

Check your x402 endpoint. Free, live, nothing to install.

Paste the URL of an x402 route you run. Our server sends it one anonymous request, never pays, and tells you what a buyer client would see.

Two answers come from that one response. First: does the payment request pass the official x402 schema, the check a real buyer client runs before it pays. A request that fails it is usually not recognised as a payment request at all, and the seller sees no error. Second: how far up the receipt ladder you get, for the levels that need no payment.

We do not store the result. The answer is kept in memory for two minutes so that a double click does not hit your server twice. A route can be checked a limited number of times per hour, and you may check only routes you run or have permission to test.

Why this exists: a payment request can look fine to the person who wrote it and still fail every real buyer, silently. We shipped exactly that ourselves on 2026-10-22: a field 53 characters long where the buyer schema allows 32, with no error anywhere on our side. This page runs the check we wished we had had.
